Datadog closed at $268.56 on September 29, up nearly 100% for the year and about 8% below its 52-week high of $292.72.
Consensus expects revenue to grow around 30% this year to about $4.5 billion, and cash from operations already passed $1 billion in fiscal 2025.
The Street's mean target of around $286 implies only around 7% upside after this year's run.
The next quarterly report will show whether growth can keep pace with a valuation near 100 times forward earnings.
Datadog (DDOG:NASDAQ) runs an observability and security platform that monitors infrastructure, applications and AI workloads.
Revenue has more than tripled since fiscal 2021, from $1.03 billion to $3.43 billion in fiscal 2025, and grew 28% last year. The chart below adds consensus estimates through fiscal 2030.
Analysts expect revenue near $4.5 billion this year, up around 30%, and around $9.4 billion by fiscal 2030, close to triple the fiscal 2025 level. Datadog's own guidance lines up: full-year revenue of $4.45 billion to $4.47 billion, after a second quarter of $1.12 billion that was up 36% from a year earlier.
Consensus has revenue growing around 26% a year over the next two years, with earnings up around 20% and EBITDA around 32%.
Because EBITDA is expected to grow fastest, analysts appear to be building in wider margins as the company gets bigger.
Cash Flow Is Strong, but GAAP Profit Is Thin
Cash flow has grown faster than sales. Cash from operations rose from $287 million in fiscal 2021 to $1.05 billion in fiscal 2025, about 31% of that year's revenue, and the chart below shows the climb. Growth slowed to 21% in fiscal 2025, though on a much larger base.
GAAP profit looks nothing like the cash flow. In the second quarter, operating income was $5 million, a margin of effectively zero, while the non-GAAP operating margin was 23%. With gross margin around 80%, the gap between gross and operating profit comes from what Datadog spends to run and grow the business.
On TIKR's numbers, trailing EBIT margin is 0.5%, which is why earnings-based multiples run high.
Should You Buy Datadog Stock?
The shares have climbed from $135.99 at the end of 2025 to $268.56, and analyst targets have risen with them. TIKR's Street Targets table shows the mean target climbing from around $139 in mid-2025 to around $286 today, with 41 of 46 analysts at Buy or Outperform and only two at Underperform or Sell.
At roughly $96.5 billion, the market value is around 19 times next year's revenue.
The bull case rests on growth: revenue that could roughly triple by 2030 and more than $1 billion in annual cash from operations. Analysts are almost uniformly positive, and net cash of about $3.7 billion adds a cushion.
The bear case starts with price. The mean target is only around 7% above the current price, the forward P/E is near 100, and the lowest target, $158, sits about 41% below the stock.
A GAAP operating margin near zero leaves little room for slower growth, and a beta near 1.5 means the shares tend to move more than the market.

Datadog Stock at $269: Is Acceleration Already Priced In After the Post-Earnings Selloff? ©bluebay2014 from Getty Images and Just_Super from Getty Images Signature via Canva
Datadog's revenue growth accelerated for five straight quarters, from 24.59% in Q1 2025 to 35.64% in Q2 2026, when sales reached $1.12 billion.
The Q3 guide of $1.135 billion to $1.145 billion implies only about 1% to 2% sequential growth because management assumed the largest customer's usage would remain at its contractual commitment level.
The NTM P/E has rebounded to 101.14x, well above its 76.82x average since January, even with the stock still about 5% below its pre-earnings close.
Datadog Stock Fell on a Guide Built Around One Customer
On the morning of August 6, Datadog (DDOG) reported the kind of quarter growth investors wait years for. Revenue rose 36% to $1.12 billion, the $115 million sequential gain was a company record by a wide margin, and customers outside the AI cohort grew in the high 20s percent, up from 18% a year earlier. By the afternoon, the stock was down 16.6% at $235.95.
The trigger sat a few lines lower. Third-quarter guidance of $1.135 billion to $1.145 billion implies 28% to 29% year-over-year growth and revenue only about 1% to 2% above Q2. After an 11% sequential jump, that looked like a wall.
Management explained the gap on the Q2 earnings call. The largest customer, which CEO Olivier Pomel described as a leading AI company, signed a nine-figure renewal but reduced its usage starting in Q3. Rather than guess how far usage would drift, Datadog guided that account at its contractual floor. "It can't go below the commitment," CFO David Obstler said at a Goldman Sachs conference in September.
The revenue chart shows what that single account is standing in front of. Growth bottomed at 24.59% in Q1 2025, then rose to 28.12%, 28.35%, 29.21%, 32.15% and 35.64% over the next five quarters. Quarterly revenue climbed from $0.76 billion to $1.12 billion across that stretch.
Pomel argued the trend barely depends on the account in question, saying that backing out the largest customer leaves "pretty much the same growth rate." New customers are also pulling more weight, accounting for about 30% of year-over-year revenue growth in Q2, up from 25% in Q1.
That does not make the guide meaningless. Usage-based revenue can fall as quickly as it rises, and Datadog learned that after the pandemic boom. Pomel told a Citi conference in September that cloud-native customers made up "about 40% of our business at peak" before spending contracted, and that exposure to AI natives today is "much smaller."
The Market Has Already Forgiven the Guide
The valuation chart shows how quickly investors came around. Datadog's NTM P/E peaked at 116.91x just before earnings, slid toward 80x by early September, and has since climbed back to 101.14x. NTM EV/Revenue sits at 18.75x, against a 21.76x high and a 13.98x average since January.
The share price has not fully followed. Datadog closed at $268.70 on September 28, about 14% above where it traded on August 6 but still roughly 5% below the $283.17 close before earnings. A multiple back near its highs with the price still below its pre-earnings level likely reflects higher forward earnings estimates after management raised full-year revenue guidance to $4.45 billion to $4.47 billion.
The results suggest the broader customer base remains strong despite the impact from the largest account. Five quarters of acceleration, a floor-based assumption for the largest account, and a guidance method that Obstler says deliberately discounts observed usage trends all leave room for Q3 to land above the range. At 101x forward earnings, though, the stock is no longer pricing a one-customer scare. It is pricing the acceleration holding.
That raises the stakes for the Q3 report. Non-AI growth staying in the high 20s and revenue clearing the $1.145 billion top end would support the rebuilt multiple. A fade in the broader customer base would be the real warning, because the guide already carries the largest customer at its contractual floor.
At 101.14x forward earnings, Datadog now needs its broader customer base to keep accelerating. Snowflake Slides 4% on Proposed $3.5B Convertible Offering; Oracle Falls 3%, Datadog Drops 4%
Snowflake's massive convertible note proposal is rattling cloud stocks across the board, but the deal's unusual structure raises a question worth answering before assuming the worst about dilution.
Published September 28, 2026, 9:45am ET · 4 min read
Market Movers desk. Editor: David Moadel.
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
A digital visualization depicts a sharp market decline, symbolizing the financial impact on hard disk drive manufacturers like Seagate and Western Digital in the wake of recent industry shifts. © 24/7 Wall Street
A $3.5 billion convertible note plan from Snowflake (NYSE:SNOW | SNOW Price Prediction) weighs on Snowflake stock. Even so, the data cloud company structured the deal specifically to limit the dilution sellers appear to be pricing in. Snowflake stock is at $321.65, down 4%, but still up 47.59% year to date.
Selling is spreading across other highly valued cloud names that have no offering of their own. Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) stock trades at $132.45, down 3%, which places the database giant inside the same pullback. Similarly, Datadog (NASDAQ:DDOG) stock is at $257.85, down 4%, a drop roughly as steep as Snowflake’s slide.
The First Trust Cloud Computing ETF (NASDAQ:SKYY) is slipping 0.9%, a far softer decline than any of those three stocks. Large-cap tech is holding up slightly better, with the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) down 0.8%. That spread points to selling concentrated in high-multiple cloud names, with Snowflake’s financing news adding a company-specific push.
Convertible Notes Designed to Cap Dilution
Under the proposal, Snowflake intends to offer the convertible senior notes in a private placement to qualified institutional buyers, subject to market conditions. The offering from Snowflake comes in two tranches maturing later this decade, and the notes carry no regular interest.
Snowflake expects to use its net proceeds for capped call transactions. It will also buy back a portion of its existing convertible notes and allocate funds for general corporate purposes, which may include share buybacks and acquisitions or strategic investments. Those capped calls are privately negotiated and are generally expected to reduce potential dilution to Snowflake common stock when the notes convert, subject to a ceiling.
Weighing Dilution Against Balance Sheet Strength
Dilution risk is the first worry for Snowflake bears, since a convertible offering expands the potential share count. Convertible arbitrage desks also routinely short Snowflake stock while buying the notes, which adds mechanical selling pressure. That overhang lands on a company already leaning heavily on equity pay, with Snowflake recording $456 million in stock-based compensation in its most recent quarter.
A more constructive read on Snowflake centers on the deal’s structure. Notes that carry no regular interest push Snowflake’s existing maturities further out and leave the company with cash for buybacks and acquisitions, so its balance sheet could end up stronger than it started. Snowflake has already shown an appetite for returning capital, buy back $300 million of common stock during the six months ended July 31.
Operating momentum at Snowflake gives that view some weight. During the second quarter of fiscal 2027, the company grew its sales 35.1% year over year to $1.55 billion and lifted its full-year product revenue guidance to $6.07 billion. However, Snowflake still posted a net loss of $191.72 million for the period, which helps explain why fresh convertible paper draws scrutiny.
Oracle and Datadog shares are falling hard even without company financing news, which frames Snowflake’s decline as one piece of a wider cloud pullback. These cloud infrastructure names belong to the same cohort. Their valuations lean heavily on growth expectations (riding a high-multiple move is fine as long as the exit is planned, and our free handbook covers both sides: here).
Datadog stock is still up 95.47% year to date, so the pullback cuts a large gain for one of the group’s strongest performers. By contrast, Oracle stock is down 31.46% year to date, and the latest drop compounds an already rough stretch.
Snowflake stands apart as the only one of the three with a company-specific financing catalyst, and convertible hedging can amplify moves in Snowflake shares, so that mix of sector drag and deal-related hedging could keep Snowflake stock more volatile than its cloud peers until the deal is finalized.
Balancing Risk and Opportunity in Snowflake
Investors may want to keep an eye on Snowflake stock once the offering prices, since the final terms and the capped call ceiling shape how much hedging pressure remains. Snowflake’s liquidity also matters, and the company finished the period with $4.3 billion in cash and investments.
Given the offering overhang, anyone considering Snowflake should keep their position moderate and add to it gradually. Shareholders who already own SNOW stock should weigh their exposure to other cloud names too, since Oracle and Datadog are slipping alongside Snowflake. Pairing their Snowflake stake with their broader cloud exposure through the First Trust Cloud Computing ETF could cushion the hit from single-company financing news.
Traders could watch for signs that Oracle and Datadog stock stabilize, since a firmer peer group could help separate Snowflake’s deal-driven selling from the wider cloud drag. Solid growth gives Snowflake’s bull case real ground, and the final pricing of the offering could shape the next leg for SNOW stock.

Jev/Datadog: 'Decision-making AI' is already entering the field | The 'd1' decision-making model that surpasses Jev
Weekly Infrastructure Observation Vol. 6
Liquid AI releases 'd1', a decision-making model that claims to 'surpass Jev'
The 'gateways' (GitHub, Hugging Face, OpenRouter, Docker) show no major changes this week.
Shortly after Jev's release, multiple independent evaluations have emerged. Even the actual call data and evaluation methods have been made public.
Datadog has released a method for using Jev to evaluate AI agents.
Anthropic's IPO-related documents reveal that it has commitments of approximately $518 billion for AI infrastructure over the next 10 years.
🎧 Highlights: This episode is packed with highlights once again
Liquid AI's 'd1', a decision-making model that claims to 'surpass Jev'
On September 29, Liquid AI released the 'd1' decision-making model. Rather than generating text, it is a model in the same vein as Jev that returns 'selections, judgments, scores,' and probabilities for given information. According to Liquid AI, it is the first model to surpass Jev on the Hugging Face Jev Decision Index. It also claims superiority in multilingual evaluation, long inputs, and resistance to prompt injection.
Independent evaluations of TypeSafe AI's 'Jev' began shortly after its release in September.
PriorBench has published evaluation results based on 5,721 calls, 21 experiments, and 50 pre-registered predictions. They are verifying latency, classification accuracy, and the handling of probabilities. While some results show that weaknesses mentioned in Jev's official documentation were not reproduced, other issues have been reported, such as the model classifying out-of-scope inputs with high confidence when a 'none of the above' option is not provided.
Another independent evaluation also published an experiment comparing Jev with small LLMs, frontier LLMs, and conventional classifiers. Both are evaluations unrelated to TypeSafe, and the code and data have been made public.
Datadog has released a method for integrating Jev into its Agent Observability platform.
Datadog is a company that provides services for recording and monitoring the actual operational status of systems and AI agents. In this instance, they are using Jev to evaluate AI agent responses based on criteria such as 'is it correct?', 'what type of failure is it?', and 'how severe is the problem?'
It supports both methods: evaluating processes that occurred in the production environment after the fact, and evaluating them in advance using datasets.
Anthropic's massive investment in AI infrastructure
Anthropic's IPO-related documents reveal that the company has committed to approximately $518 billion in AI infrastructure-related obligations over the next decade.
The breakdown includes major contracts with Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and others, many of which are non-cancellable obligations regardless of usage.
While Anthropic is projected to generate approximately $4.6 billion in revenue in 2025, its net loss is approximately $42 billion. The competition is not just about developing AI models, but has also grown into a massive investment race to secure computing resources.
Two weeks ago, I wrote about Jev, noting that 'there is no third-party verification yet.' In two weeks, that has changed.
Moreover, it's not just about measuring performance; moves to integrate Jev into other AI systems for evaluation have already begun. This is interesting.
Specialized tools are becoming necessary not only for those building AI agents, but also for those measuring whether AI agents are working properly. Meanwhile, at Anthropic, the discussion about how to secure computing resources has become even larger than the talk about the models themselves.
AI competition seems to be shifting from a stage of competing solely on model performance to competition over the entire foundation that runs, evaluates, combines, and supports models. Looking at 'd1,' I have a strong feeling that AI required for development sites—specifically decision-making models—will continue to emerge from here on out. We are currently looking at the entrance to that era.
Next week, I want to look at how much Jev is actually starting to be used in real products and agents.

Fortinet vs. Datadog: Which Cloud Security Stock Has Better Potential?
Zacks Investment Research - Zacks Investment Research - Tue Sep 22, 9:12AM CDT
Fortinet Inc.FTNT is a leading cybersecurity provider focused on secure networking, firewalls, SASE and AI-driven security operations. Datadog, Inc.DDOG offers a cloud-native observability and security platform that helps enterprises monitor and protect applications, infrastructure and increasingly AI workloads.
Both companies are positioned to benefit from rising enterprise spending on cybersecurity, cloud migration and AI infrastructure. The comparison is particularly timely after strong second-quarter 2026 results, as both companies have demonstrated potential for future top-line growth. Their strong growth profiles but distinct security strategies make FTNT and DDOG worth comparing for investors seeking exposure to enterprise security.
Fortinet is positioned to benefit from rising enterprise spending on cybersecurity as cloud migration, AI deployment and distributed infrastructure expand attack surfaces. Its SASE Firewall combines firewall, SD-WAN and SASE capabilities on a single FortiOS platform, supporting security across data centers, cloud environments and remote users. Fortinet says its approach allows both cloud and sovereign, on-premises SASE deployment, giving customers flexibility around performance, data residency and compliance.
The growth opportunity is supported by Fortinet's large installed base and expanding portfolio. The company has more than 900K lifetime customers, 110K partners and $8.6 billion in LTM billings. Its second-quarter presentation identifies a $148 billion 2029 SASE Firewall TAM, with a 13% 2025-2029 CAGR, while AI security represents a $172 billion opportunity. The company is also gaining traction in customer deployments. A cloud provider selected Fortinet to secure generative-AI data centers in an eight-figure deal, while a global pharmaceutical company signed a seven-figure FortiSASE deal covering more than 45K users.
Second-quarter 2026 results demonstrate strong momentum. Revenues increased 26% to $2.05 billion, product revenues jumped 52% to $773 million, and billings rose 33% to $2.37 billion. FortiSASE billings grew more than 100%, while Unified SASE billings increased 35%, and free cash flow reached $966 million, with a 38% non-GAAP operating margin.
Fortinet is also deepening its AI-security ecosystem through collaborations with Intel, Anthropic, OpenAI and NVIDIA. Its portfolio includes Lacework FortiCNAPP, adding to its broader cloud-security capabilities.
FTNT's combination of recurring services, strong cash generation, broad customer reach and integrated SASE/AI security provides multiple avenues for growth. Fortinet raised its 2026 revenue outlook to $8.02-$8.18 billion, representing 19% year-over-year growth at the midpoint. Investors should also monitor competition, the timing of large enterprise deals and the risk that technological changes, including advances in AI, could affect product competitiveness.
The Zacks Consensus Estimate for FTNT’s 2026 earnings is pegged at $3.42 per share, up by 2 cents over the past 30 days, implying approximately 23.9% year-over-year growth.
Datadog offers investors exposure to rising enterprise spending on cloud migration, cybersecurity and AI workloads through its AI-powered observability and security platform. Its unified SaaS platform integrates infrastructure monitoring, application performance, log management, cloud security and other capabilities, allowing customers to secure and monitor their technology stacks from a common platform. This creates an opportunity for Datadog to expand revenues as customers add workloads and adopt additional products across their technology environments.
DDOG's customer base provides a meaningful expansion opportunity. The second quarter ended with approximately 33,400 customers, including 4,720 customers generating at least $100,000 in ARR, up from 3,850 a year earlier. These larger customers contributed about 91% of ARR, while adoption of four or more products increased to 58% from 52%. Its security portfolio includes Cloud Security, Code Security, Cloud SIEM and Data Security, strengthening its positioning as enterprises consolidate monitoring and security workloads.
Recent customer wins reinforce this strategy. A South American bank signed a seven-figure annualized deal and adopted Cloud SIEM and Data Security, while a Fortune 100 health insurer expanded toward 19 Datadog products, citing HIPAA compliance, PII handling and Cloud SIEM as differentiators. A multiyear deal worth more than $30 million in TCV also displaced four existing tools.
Financially, second-quarter 2026 revenues increased 36% to $1.12 billion, while free cash flow reached $279 million. Datadog guided for 2026 revenues of $4.45-$4.47 billion.
However, competition remains intense, with Datadog facing established vendors, cloud-provider solutions and lower-priced alternatives. Security breaches, service disruptions, changing privacy regulations, AI-related risks and reduced enterprise IT spending could also pressure growth.
The Zacks Consensus Estimate for DDOG’s 2026 earnings is currently pegged at $2.52 per share, implying approximately 22.9% year-over-year growth. Earnings estimates have remained stable over the past 30 days.
Over the past three months, shares of FTNT have gained 18.4% compared with DDOG’s 11.1% rise. Fortinet’s outperformance is backed by a more favorable near-term execution narrative, with accelerating billings, robust product demand, strong cash generation and raised 2026 guidance.
By comparison, DDOG continues to post strong growth and AI momentum, but management flagged a major customer’s user reduction beginning in the third quarter of 2026, creating a near-term growth consideration.
Fortinet’s valuation is relatively more moderate than Datadog’s despite both stocks carrying a Value Score of F. FTNT trades at a 17.22X trailing 12-month Price/Sales multiple, compared with 22.92X for DDOG. FTNT’s low multiple indicates that there is strong upside potential for higher profits if growth remains intact.
Fortinet and Datadog both offer strong exposure to cybersecurity, cloud migration and AI-driven spending. FTNT combines faster billings growth, robust free cash flow, raised 2026 guidance, a broad installed base and a lower Price/Sales multiple. DDOG continues to deliver strong revenue growth and expanding product adoption, but faces near-term customer-related pressure.
Given these factors, FTNT seems a better pick for investors than DDOG right now. While Fortinet sports a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy) at present, Datadog has a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold).

Radical New Technology Could Hand Investors Huge Gains
Quantum Computing is the next technological revolution, and it could be even more advanced than AI.
While some believed the technology was years away, it is already present and moving fast. Large hyperscalers, such as Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Oracle, and even Meta and Tesla, are scrambling to integrate quantum computing into their infrastructure.

Kevin was among the early experts who recognized NVIDIA's enormous potential back in 2016. Now, he has keyed in on what could be "the next big thing" in quantum computing supremacy. Today, you have a rare chance to position your portfolio at the forefront of this opportunity.

Datadog traded near record levels on artificial intelligence-driven cloud demand as October opened.
The observability platform grows through broad expansion within its existing customer base.
A cooler inflation reading supported richly valued cloud software names.
opened October trading near record levels on artificial intelligence-driven cloud demand, with a fresh favorable initiation adding to the upbeat tone as the S&P 500 edged higher following a softer inflation reading.
The timing placed one of the clearest proxies for cloud spending at the center of the growth conversation, with broad customer expansion and questions about concentration both shaping the narrative.
Cloud software opened October on steadier footing as the S&P 500 edged higher following a cooler inflation reading. Within the growth category, observability names that help companies keep sprawling digital systems running drew renewed attention, and Datadog sat prominently among them.
Observability has become a staple line in the technology budget as organizations move more of their operations to the cloud and layer artificial intelligence on top. The more complex a company's digital footprint becomes, the more it needs tools to watch over it, a dynamic that underpins the demand for Datadog.
The softer inflation print eased pressure on yields, lending support to the richly valued end of the market where fast-growing cloud software resides. That tailwind framed the opening of the quarter for the category.
Datadog provides a monitoring and observability platform that lets organizations see how their software, servers and cloud systems are performing in real time. When an application slows or a system falters, the platform helps engineering teams pinpoint the trouble quickly.
The company began with infrastructure monitoring and steadily broadened into a wide suite that spans application performance, log management, security monitoring and more. That expansion turned a single tool into a platform that touches many corners of a customer's technology operations.
The breadth matters because it lets Datadog grow within each account. A customer that starts with one product often adds others over time, which lifts the revenue each relationship generates and deepens the platform's role in daily operations.
As October opened, Datadog traded near record levels following a strong post-earnings reset and a fresh wave of upbeat coverage. Recent reporting centered on artificial intelligence-driven product demand, broad customer expansion and the company's standing as a core cloud software name.
The narrative has not been one-directional. Coverage also flagged questions about how the market prices the stock and about reliance on a concentrated set of very large customers, a reminder that even strong growth names carry open questions.
A new favorable initiation added to the upbeat tone, while the stock's history of sharp swings underscored how sensitive the name remains to shifts in sentiment. The mix of momentum and debate kept Datadog squarely in focus.
Artificial Intelligence as a Demand Driver
Artificial intelligence has become a meaningful thread in the Datadog story. As companies build and run artificial intelligence applications, they generate vast new streams of data and new systems that must be watched, expanding the work observability platforms are asked to do.
Datadog has leaned into that shift with tools aimed at monitoring artificial intelligence workloads and the infrastructure behind them. The pitch is that the more artificial intelligence a company deploys, the more it needs visibility into how those systems behave.
That linkage ties the company to one of the market's most watched themes. Rising artificial intelligence adoption translates into more systems to monitor, which feeds directly into the demand that drives Datadog's expansion.
The growth category gathers together the fast-expanding names that the market prizes for their trajectory rather than their present scale, and Datadog sits firmly among them. The firm's blend of rapid revenue expansion and a central role in cloud operations places it near the front of the group.
Within the broader Growth Stocks space on kalkinemedia.com, the company remains one of the names that market watchers track most closely as the growth category navigates a shifting rate backdrop. Datadog shares trade on the Nasdaq, placing the stock within the Nasdaq Composite.
That placement shapes how the market treats each update, since names in the category are judged against a high bar for sustained expansion. A steady stream of product launches and broad customer adoption keeps the company anchored in the conversation about where cloud software heads next.
A defining feature of Datadog is its usage-based model. Rather than charging a flat subscription, the company bills in large part according to how much customers consume, which means revenue scales with the activity flowing through a customer's systems.
That model cuts both ways. When customers grow and run more workloads, Datadog revenue climbs alongside them, a powerful tailwind during periods of expansion. When customers trim consumption to control costs, the same mechanism can slow growth.
The sensitivity to customer activity makes the company a useful window into cloud spending trends. Its commentary on consumption patterns is read closely for clues about how broadly organizations are expanding their digital operations.
Datadog's growth has leaned heavily on expansion within its existing base, with customers steadily adopting more of its products over time. That land-and-expand pattern is central to the story and reflects the platform's deepening role in technology operations.
At the same time, coverage has flagged reliance on a concentrated set of very large customers, whose consumption decisions can sway results. A pullback in spending by a handful of major accounts can ripple through the numbers in a way that draws scrutiny.
Balancing broad adoption against that concentration is an ongoing theme. The breadth of its product suite helps, since it spreads each relationship across many tools, but the influence of the largest accounts remains a point the market watches.
Datadog operates in a competitive arena. It faces large cloud providers that offer their own monitoring tools, other independent observability vendors, and open-source options that some organizations prefer to run themselves.
The company's answer has been breadth and integration. By offering a single platform that spans many monitoring needs, it aims to spare customers the task of stitching together separate tools, a pitch that resonates with teams managing complex systems.
That integrated approach is central to the growth story. Each additional product a customer adopts deepens the relationship and raises the cost of switching, strengthening the company's standing against both cloud giants and niche rivals.
Datadog carries a premium market-value profile, a reflection of its growth rates, its expanding product suite and its ties to the artificial intelligence theme. That premium raises the bar for each update, since the stock is priced for sustained expansion.
When a name trades at such levels, the market reacts sharply to any shift in the growth trajectory. The stock has a history of pronounced swings around earnings, and recent coverage noted a sharp pullback tied to concentration concerns even amid strong results.
For the growth category, Datadog often serves as a gauge of appetite for premium cloud software. Its action tends to track the broader mood toward names that pair rapid expansion with rich market values.
Several challenges accompany the Datadog story. The usage-based model, while powerful in good times, exposes the company to customers trimming consumption when budgets tighten. Reliance on a concentrated set of large accounts adds to that sensitivity.
Competition from cloud giants that bundle monitoring into their platforms remains persistent, and the company's premium standing leaves little room for disappointment. Maintaining the pace of product adoption that fuels expansion requires constant development.
These challenges temper but do not erase the firm's momentum. They frame the uncertainty that travels alongside a fast-growing, richly valued cloud software name.
Datadog occupies a distinctive spot in the cloud software landscape. By building a single platform that unifies many monitoring needs, it has positioned itself as an alternative to the patchwork of separate tools that engineering teams once stitched together.
That positioning has resonated with organizations managing increasingly complex systems, who value a single place to see how everything is performing. The company frames its platform as the connective tissue that ties scattered signals into one coherent picture.
The breadth of the suite reinforces that standing. As a customer adopts more products, the platform becomes more deeply woven into daily operations, raising the cost of switching and strengthening the relationship over time.
Serving organizations of many sizes and industries broadens the company's reach across the market. That span is central to how the name is framed within the growth category.
Among the developments drawing attention has been the steady expansion of the platform's product lineup, which widens the range of monitoring needs a single vendor can address. Each addition gives customers another reason to consolidate onto the platform.
The push into monitoring artificial intelligence workloads has featured prominently, tying the company to one of the market's most watched themes. As organizations deploy more artificial intelligence systems, the need for visibility into how they behave grows alongside.
A strong post-earnings reset and a fresh favorable initiation have shaped the recent tone, even as coverage flagged the stock's rich market value and reliance on a concentrated set of large accounts. That mix of momentum and debate has kept the name squarely in focus.
Industry Developments Shaping the Backdrop
The cloud software industry has spent the opening of the quarter absorbing a wave of artificial intelligence activity, from expanded computing commitments by the largest technology firms to a flood of new applications that generate fresh data to watch. That current keeps demand for observability near the top of the corporate agenda.
Datadog sits downstream of those developments. As organizations build and run more artificial intelligence systems, the volume of signals that must be monitored climbs, and the need for a platform that can make sense of it all grows more pressing. The company has framed itself as the natural home for that work.
The industry backdrop also features a steady march toward more complex, distributed systems. As technology estates grow more tangled, the value of a single platform that can watch over the whole of it rises, and the company has leaned into that trend as a core part of its pitch.

Can Datadog’s (DDOG) Platform Keep Growing as Companies Embrace AI?
Tue, September 29, 2026 at 9:38 PM PDT 4 min read
Datadog, Inc. (NASDAQ:DDOG) has spent years building a business around a simple problem: modern software is becoming harder to manage. Companies now run applications across clouds, containers, databases, and increasingly complex infrastructure, creating more data and more things that can go wrong.
AI is adding another layer to that complexity. But the opportunity is broader than AI alone. The company's non-AI customer base is actually accelerating, while AI is creating new workloads that need to be monitored, secured, and managed.
DON'T MISS: Jim Cramer Explained Datadog, Inc. (NASDAQ:DDOG)'s Share Price Movement
Can Datadog's (DDOG) Platform Keep Growing as Companies Embrace AI?
Datadog's management sees AI as benefiting the business in several ways. More AI workloads mean more cloud usage, which creates more activity for Datadog's existing products. At the same time, AI applications introduce new things companies need to track, from GPUs and LLMs to autonomous agents and the tools those agents use.
That is already showing up in customer activity. More than 750 AI-focused customers were using Datadog in the second quarter, including major companies building their own AI infrastructure. Management also said activity from AI agents is growing rapidly, with MCP tool calls increasing more than 22-fold from the end of 2025.
But perhaps the more encouraging trend is what is happening outside AI. Revenue growth among Datadog's broader customer base, excluding AI customers, accelerated to the high-20% range in the second quarter, up from 18% a year earlier. That suggests customers are spending more on cloud and modern software infrastructure even without an AI-related boost.
The other trend worth watching is how much more of the platform customers are using.
Datadog, Inc. (NASDAQ:DDOG) started with infrastructure monitoring, but it now offers more than 20 products spanning observability, security, cloud costs, and application management. About 85% of customers were using at least two products by June, while 37% were using six or more.
That matters because Datadog doesn't necessarily need to win an entirely new customer every time it wants to grow. It can expand within an existing account.
Management gave a good example: one large media customer signed a multiyear deal worth more than $30 million after choosing Datadog across its business and replacing four commercial and internal tools. The customer was using 19 Datadog products.
That kind of expansion could become increasingly important as companies try to simplify their software stacks.
READ ALSO: Datadog (DDOG) Grows Fast, Then Gets Punished For Slowing Down
The valuation leaves little room for disappointment
The market clearly sees the opportunity. Datadog's shares have risen sharply, and the stock was trading at roughly 84.8x forward earnings after surging more than 75% since May. Analysts expect adjusted EPS to grow about 23% in 2026, according to current consensus estimates.
The company needs to keep doing two things at once: grow revenue quickly and show that more of that growth can eventually translate into durable profits.
Datadog's platform appears well positioned to keep growing as companies adopt AI and manage increasingly complicated software environments. The encouraging part is that the opportunity isn't dependent entirely on AI. Existing customers are expanding their use of Datadog, non-AI demand is accelerating, and new AI workloads are opening additional areas for the company to serve.
The biggest concern is the price. At around 85x forward earnings, Datadog already has a lot of growth baked into the stock. The business has plenty of room to grow, but it will need to keep winning customers, expanding within existing accounts, and turning that growth into higher profits to make that valuation look reasonable.
Market sentiment toward Datadog strengthened in Insider Monkey's database. The number of hedge funds holding the stock increased from 80 at the end of Q1 to 92 at the end of Q2 2026, while the total value of their positions jumped from about $2.54 billion to $3.94 billion over the same period.
While we acknowledge the potential of DDOG as an investment, we believe certain AI stocks offer greater upside potential and carry less downside risk. Datadog Climbs 6%, Approaches 52-Week High While Software Group Slips; Oracle and Cloudflare Decline
Datadog is surging while its closest rival and the broader software sector both slide lower, a split that raises a pointed question about whether this rally reflects genuine conviction or a momentum trade at a dangerously rich valuation.
Published September 25, 2026, 2:06pm ET · 4 min read
Market Movers desk. Editor: David Moadel.
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.

Datadog (NASDAQ:DDOG | DDOG Price Prediction) stock is up 6% to $272.50, a sharp gain for the observability and monitoring company. That strength arrives against a weaker software group, giving Datadog stock a move that belongs to it alone.
Across software, the iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF (NYSEARCA:IGV) is down 0.4%, which puts Datadog stock on the opposite side of its own sector. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) is up 0.5%, so the broad market is slightly higher while software lags behind it.
At the same time, Dynatrace (NYSE:DT) stock is down 0.8% to $58.23, a mild slip for the company Datadog competes with most directly in observability. Taken together, those three readings describe a single-stock rally, with Datadog stock carrying the move on its own shoulders.
Datadog stock is climbing while Dynatrace stock and the software fund are both falling, a split that points to buying aimed squarely at this one name, and a gain of this size traces back to demand for Datadog specifically when a software fund slips and a direct observability competitor slides alongside it.
Isolated strength in Datadog stock can reflect conviction in the platform’s long-run staying power, since buyers are paying up for one monitoring provider while passing on Dynatrace stock. Such concentrated rallies can also fade once enthusiasm cools off, which is why the valuation behind Datadog stock deserves a closer look.
Checking in on some of Datadog’s other peers, Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) stock is down 0.77% to $138.46. Meanwhile, Cloudflare (NYSE:NET) stock is slipping 2% to $350.77.
Over the past 52 weeks, Datadog stock has traded between a low of $98.01 and a high of $292.72. Those two figures frame the year Datadog shareholders have lived through, and they give investors a way to judge the current price against both extremes.
Datadog stock trades at a trailing P/E ratio of 504x, a multiple built on very thin profit over the past year. On a forward basis, the ratio is 85x, and that number depends on earnings Datadog hasn’t reported yet. Each ratio captures a different slice of the Datadog story, one looking back and the other looking ahead.
Paying up for growth is a familiar pattern in software, and Datadog stock is priced like a company expected to keep expanding its profit base. Any stumble in execution could pressure a multiple this rich, while steady delivery could help justify it. These figures leave it unclear whether Datadog can grow into that multiple quickly enough to support a price at these levels.
Bulls point to a monitoring platform that keeps growing, with the market willing to pay a premium for that consistency. Datadog sells an analytics and monitoring platform for developers, information technology operations teams and business users, a broad audience that gives it several ways to strengthen customer relationships.
During Datadog’s August 6 earnings call, the company’s leadership struck an positive tone on demand. “Overall, we continue to see healthy trends in customer demand,” stated Olivier Pomel, Datadog’s co-founder and chief executive at the time of the call. Management also disclosed a usage reduction at Datadog’s largest customer. The chief financial officer declared that the company had “fully de-risked” guidance with respect to that account.
Skeptics can point to the valuation, since a multiple in the hundreds on trailing profit leaves Datadog stock little room for disappointment. A usage cut at one large account also shows how shifts in concentrated spending can affect the outlook for a company priced for steady expansion. Momentum-driven buying tends to attract late buyers as enthusiasm peaks, adding another layer of risk around Datadog stock.
Investors may want to watch for Datadog’s next quarterly report, which could show whether profits are catching up to the forward multiple. Holding the gain in the days ahead could also reveal how durable this burst of buying proves to be. Calm follow-through would suggest steady accumulation, while a quick giveback would point to short-term trading around Datadog stock.
Given the rich multiple, anyone adding to their Datadog exposure should size their positions carefully. Existing holders should weigh their risk tolerance against a valuation that leaves Datadog stock sensitive to any slowdown. Spreading their exposure across several software names could help cushion a sharp reversal in any single holding.
Datadog stock carries its own gain while the software fund and Dynatrace stock drift lower, which sets it apart in its corner of the market. Shareholders could keep an eye on Datadog stock relative to its 52-week high, since that level has limited the shares over the past year.

What Happened?
Shares of cloud monitoring platform Datadog (NASDAQ:DDOG) jumped 5.9% in the afternoon session after Wedbush initiated coverage of the company with an Outperform rating per TipRanks.
An Outperform rating signals to the market that the analysts expect the stock to deliver better returns than the broader market and its software industry peers over the coming months. This bullish initiation from a major brokerage drew fresh investor attention to Datadog's comprehensive enterprise observability platform, validating the company's competitive position and prompting buyers to bid the shares higher in early trading.
Notably, the magnitude of today's move builds upon a steady climb over the past couple of days, serving as a powerful continuation of a broader pre-earnings rally. As the company approaches its upcoming quarterly earnings report, this growing technical momentum suggests that investors were already actively accumulating positions, with the Wedbush upgrade acting as a high-conviction catalyst to accelerate the ongoing upward trend.
Ultimately, this sustained pre-earnings run-up indicates that Wall Street is aggressively pricing in strong anticipated demand for the company's software tools, using the positive initiation note as fundamental justification to confidently increase exposure ahead of the print.

Datadog's shares are extremely volatile and have had 39 moves greater than 5% over the last year. In that context, today's move indicates the market considers this news meaningful but not something that would fundamentally change its perception of the business.
The previous big move we wrote about was 4 days ago when the stock gained 4.5% on the news that falling Treasury yields eased pressure on software stocks as signs of cooler U.S.–China tensions lifted risk appetite. The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield fell roughly 3 basis points to 4.97%, slipping below the 5% threshold, according to CNBC. A retreat in bond yields provides relief for enterprise software equities, whose valuations are anchored by cash flows projected years into the future.
Separately, attention turned to the U.S.–China summit later in the week, slated to cover trade relations, artificial intelligence cooperation, and other geopolitical issues. The prospect of constructive talks on cross-border trade and technology policy helped ease that uncertainty and lifted risk appetite for software names.

CSCO's Security Growth Accelerates: Can It Outpace DDOG & CRWD?
Mon, September 28, 2026 at 8:35 AM PDT 3 min read
Cisco Systems CSCO is benefiting from growing enterprise adoption of integrated security and observability solutions as artificial intelligence (AI), distributed applications and increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks expand IT complexity. CSCO is combining networking with security through Secure Access, XDR, Hypershield and AI Defense, while Splunk and ThousandEyes strengthen its observability and network-assurance capabilities. The integrated approach enhances CSCO's ability to address customers seeking unified visibility and protection across networks, applications, users, and AI agents, while reinforcing its competitive positioning against Datadog DDOG and CrowdStrike CRWD.
Customer adoption is gaining momentum. CSCO's entire security portfolio, including Splunk, recorded double-digit order growth in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026. More than 1,500 customers purchased newer offerings such as Secure Access, XDR, Hypershield and AI Defense during the quarter, taking total net new customers since launch to more than 6,400. Firewall orders increased more than 30% year over year, while management highlighted that customers are increasingly seeking unified protection across users, applications and AI agents.
CSCO is also broadening its AI-driven operations capabilities. In the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, nearly 4,500 enterprises had signed up for Cisco Cloud Control, while Resilient Infrastructure Services, powered by Cisco IQ, had more than 8,600 customers. CSCO also launched Antares, a family of open-weight small language models designed to identify known code vulnerabilities.
The momentum is beginning to support financial growth. In the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, Security revenues rose 14% year over year to $2.23 billion, while Observability revenues increased 6% to $275 million. For fiscal 2026, Security revenues grew 2% to $8.23 billion, while Observability revenues increased 4% to $1.10 billion. Observability growth was driven by network assurance, partly offset by weakness in CSCO's observability-suite offerings.
Datadog is expanding from traditional cloud observability into AI-focused monitoring and security. More than 750 AI customers use DDOG, including all 10 top AI leaders. Its portfolio includes GPU Monitoring, Agent Observability, Agent Console, Data Observability and AI Guard. Datadog is also pushing deeper into security through AI Guard and Bits Security Analyst, which can operate with non-Datadog SIEM platforms. In the second quarter of fiscal 2026, platform adoption continued to deepen, with 58% of customers using four or more products and 37% using six or more products.
CrowdStrike is challenging CSCO through the continued expansion of its Falcon platform. The company reported next-generation SIEM annual recurring revenues (ARR) of more than $695 million, cloud security ARR above $905 million and identity ARR exceeding $585 million in the second quarter of fiscal 2027. Falcon Flex ARR surpassed $2.29 billion, up 101% year over year. CRWD is also seeing deeper platform consolidation, with 51% of subscription customers using six modules, 35% using seven and 26% using eight or more. This growing adoption across SIEM, endpoint, cloud, identity and AI security is increasing competitive pressure on CSCO's integrated security and observability strategy.

CSCO stock is trading at a premium, with forward 12-month price/earnings of 20.56X compared with the broader sector's 21.27X. Cisco Systems has a Value Score of F.

Datadog Stock Has Nearly Doubled This Year, but Wall Street Sees Only About 7% More Upside
Tue, September 29, 2026 at 5:11 PM PDT 3 min read
Datadog Stock Has Nearly Doubled This Year, but Wall Street Sees Only About 7% More Upside ©vaeenma from Getty Images, flyparade from Getty Images Signature via Canva
Datadog closed at $268.56 on September 29, up nearly 100% for the year and about 8% below its 52-week high of $292.72.
Consensus expects revenue to grow around 30% this year to about $4.5 billion, and cash from operations already passed $1 billion in fiscal 2025.
The Street's mean target of around $286 implies only around 7% upside after this year's run.
The next quarterly report will show whether growth can keep pace with a valuation near 100 times forward earnings.
Datadog (DDOG:NASDAQ) runs an observability and security platform that monitors infrastructure, applications and AI workloads.
Revenue has more than tripled since fiscal 2021, from $1.03 billion to $3.43 billion in fiscal 2025, and grew 28% last year. The chart below adds consensus estimates through fiscal 2030.
Analysts expect revenue near $4.5 billion this year, up around 30%, and around $9.4 billion by fiscal 2030, close to triple the fiscal 2025 level. Datadog's own guidance lines up: full-year revenue of $4.45 billion to $4.47 billion, after a second quarter of $1.12 billion that was up 36% from a year earlier.
Consensus has revenue growing around 26% a year over the next two years, with earnings up around 20% and EBITDA around 32%.
Because EBITDA is expected to grow fastest, analysts appear to be building in wider margins as the company gets bigger.
Cash Flow Is Strong, but GAAP Profit Is Thin
Cash flow has grown faster than sales. Cash from operations rose from $287 million in fiscal 2021 to $1.05 billion in fiscal 2025, about 31% of that year's revenue, and the chart below shows the climb. Growth slowed to 21% in fiscal 2025, though on a much larger base.
GAAP profit looks nothing like the cash flow. In the second quarter, operating income was $5 million, a margin of effectively zero, while the non-GAAP operating margin was 23%. With gross margin around 80%, the gap between gross and operating profit comes from what Datadog spends to run and grow the business.
On TIKR's numbers, trailing EBIT margin is 0.5%, which is why earnings-based multiples run high.
Should You Buy Datadog Stock?
The shares have climbed from $135.99 at the end of 2025 to $268.56, and analyst targets have risen with them. TIKR's Street Targets table shows the mean target climbing from around $139 in mid-2025 to around $286 today, with 41 of 46 analysts at Buy or Outperform and only two at Underperform or Sell.
At roughly $96.5 billion, the market value is around 19 times next year's revenue.
The bull case rests on growth: revenue that could roughly triple by 2030 and more than $1 billion in annual cash from operations. Analysts are almost uniformly positive, and net cash of about $3.7 billion adds a cushion.
The bear case starts with price. The mean target is only around 7% above the current price, the forward P/E is near 100, and the lowest target, $158, sits about 41% below the stock.
A GAAP operating margin near zero leaves little room for slower growth, and a beta near 1.5 means the shares tend to move more than the market.

Datadog Stock at $269: Is Acceleration Already Priced In After the Post-Earnings Selloff?
Mon, September 28, 2026 at 3:09 PM PDT 4 min read
Datadog Stock at $269: Is Acceleration Already Priced In After the Post-Earnings Selloff? ©bluebay2014 from Getty Images and Just_Super from Getty Images Signature via Canva
Datadog's revenue growth accelerated for five straight quarters, from 24.59% in Q1 2025 to 35.64% in Q2 2026, when sales reached $1.12 billion.
The Q3 guide of $1.135 billion to $1.145 billion implies only about 1% to 2% sequential growth because management assumed the largest customer's usage would remain at its contractual commitment level.
The NTM P/E has rebounded to 101.14x, well above its 76.82x average since January, even with the stock still about 5% below its pre-earnings close.
Datadog Stock Fell on a Guide Built Around One Customer
On the morning of August 6, Datadog (DDOG) reported the kind of quarter growth investors wait years for. Revenue rose 36% to $1.12 billion, the $115 million sequential gain was a company record by a wide margin, and customers outside the AI cohort grew in the high 20s percent, up from 18% a year earlier. By the afternoon, the stock was down 16.6% at $235.95.
The trigger sat a few lines lower. Third-quarter guidance of $1.135 billion to $1.145 billion implies 28% to 29% year-over-year growth and revenue only about 1% to 2% above Q2. After an 11% sequential jump, that looked like a wall.
Management explained the gap on the Q2 earnings call. The largest customer, which CEO Olivier Pomel described as a leading AI company, signed a nine-figure renewal but reduced its usage starting in Q3. Rather than guess how far usage would drift, Datadog guided that account at its contractual floor. "It can't go below the commitment," CFO David Obstler said at a Goldman Sachs conference in September.
The revenue chart shows what that single account is standing in front of. Growth bottomed at 24.59% in Q1 2025, then rose to 28.12%, 28.35%, 29.21%, 32.15% and 35.64% over the next five quarters. Quarterly revenue climbed from $0.76 billion to $1.12 billion across that stretch.
Pomel argued the trend barely depends on the account in question, saying that backing out the largest customer leaves "pretty much the same growth rate." New customers are also pulling more weight, accounting for about 30% of year-over-year revenue growth in Q2, up from 25% in Q1.
That does not make the guide meaningless. Usage-based revenue can fall as quickly as it rises, and Datadog learned that after the pandemic boom. Pomel told a Citi conference in September that cloud-native customers made up "about 40% of our business at peak" before spending contracted, and that exposure to AI natives today is "much smaller."
The Market Has Already Forgiven the Guide
The valuation chart shows how quickly investors came around. Datadog's NTM P/E peaked at 116.91x just before earnings, slid toward 80x by early September, and has since climbed back to 101.14x. NTM EV/Revenue sits at 18.75x, against a 21.76x high and a 13.98x average since January.
The share price has not fully followed. Datadog closed at $268.70 on September 28, about 14% above where it traded on August 6 but still roughly 5% below the $283.17 close before earnings. A multiple back near its highs with the price still below its pre-earnings level likely reflects higher forward earnings estimates after management raised full-year revenue guidance to $4.45 billion to $4.47 billion.
The results suggest the broader customer base remains strong despite the impact from the largest account. Five quarters of acceleration, a floor-based assumption for the largest account, and a guidance method that Obstler says deliberately discounts observed usage trends all leave room for Q3 to land above the range. At 101x forward earnings, though, the stock is no longer pricing a one-customer scare. It is pricing the acceleration holding.
That raises the stakes for the Q3 report. Non-AI growth staying in the high 20s and revenue clearing the $1.145 billion top end would support the rebuilt multiple. A fade in the broader customer base would be the real warning, because the guide already carries the largest customer at its contractual floor.
At 101.14x forward earnings, Datadog now needs its broader customer base to keep accelerating. Monitor DDOG valuation multiples and estimate revisions on TIKR for free →

Datadog Announces Second Quarter 2026 Financial Results
Second quarter revenue grew 36% year-over-year to $1.12 billion
Robust growth of larger customers, with about 4,720 $100k+ ARR customers, up from about 3,850 a year ago
Launched AI-powered Bits Code, Bits Chat, and Bits Agent Builder for general availability
NEW YORK-- Datadog, Inc. (NASDAQ:DDOG), the leading AI-powered observability and security platform, today announced financial results for its second quarter ended June 30, 2026.
"Datadog delivered a strong quarter, with 36% year-over-year revenue growth, $316 million in operating cash flow, and $279 million in free cash flow," said Olivier Pomel, co-founder and CEO of Datadog. "Our customers are building and deploying with AI, and they are using the Datadog platform to observe, secure, and act on their AI-enabled solutions."
Pomel added, "We are innovating rapidly to help our customers manage rising complexity, and increasingly build autonomy into their operations."
Second Quarter 2026 Financial Highlights:
•Revenue was $1.12 billion, an increase of 36% year-over-year.
•GAAP operating income was $5 million; GAAP operating margin was 0%.
•Non-GAAP operating income was $257 million; non-GAAP operating margin was 23%.
•GAAP net income per diluted share was $0.12; non-GAAP net income per diluted share was $0.65.
•Operating cash flow was $316 million, with free cash flow of $279 million.
•Cash, cash equivalents, and marketable securities were $5.0 billion as of June 30, 2026.
Second Quarter & Recent Business Highlights:
•As of June 30, 2026, we had about 4,720 customers with ARR of $100,000 or more, an increase of 23% from about 3,850 as of June 30, 2025.
•Named a Leader in the Gartner Magic Quadrant for Observability Platforms, 2026. This is the sixth consecutive year Gartner has positioned Datadog as a Leader in the Magic Quadrant.
•Acquired Adaptive ML, a frontier AI startup developing the world’s first Reinforcement Learning Operations platform, to accelerate Datadog AI Research’s investment in world models and agentic LLM post-training for observability—combining Datadog’s access to real-world infrastructure and security data with Adaptive ML’s expertise in building specialized, high-performance AI agents.
•Launched more than 100 new capabilities at DASH 2026 to help customers drive autonomy and manage growing AI and security complexity. Highlights included fully autonomous Bits AI for end-to-end incident detection, investigation, and remediation; AI Guard to protect AI agents from prompt injection and poisoning attacks; Bring Your Own Cloud for deploying Datadog within customer environments; and Bits Agent Builder for creating custom AI agents.
Third Quarter and Full Year 2026 Outlook:
Based on information as of today, August 6, 2026, Datadog is providing the following guidance:
•Third Quarter 2026 Outlook:
◦Revenue between $1.135 billion and $1.145 billion.
◦Non-GAAP operating income between $260 million and $270 million.
◦Non-GAAP net income per share between $0.63 and $0.65, assuming approximately 378 million weighted average diluted shares outstanding.
•Full Year 2026 Outlook:
◦Revenue between $4.45 billion and $4.47 billion.
◦Non-GAAP operating income between $1.01 billion and $1.03 billion.
◦Non-GAAP net income per share between $2.50 and $2.54, assuming approximately 376 million weighted average diluted shares outstanding.
Datadog has not reconciled its expectations as to non-GAAP operating income, or as to non-GAAP net income per share, to their most directly comparable GAAP measure as a result of uncertainty regarding, and the potential variability of, reconciling items such as stock-based compensation and employer payroll taxes on equity incentive plans. Accordingly, reconciliation is not available without unreasonable effort, although it is important to note that these factors could be material to Datadog’s results computed in accordance with GAAP.
Conference Call Details:
•What: Datadog financial results for the second quarter of 2026 and outlook for the third quarter and the full year 2026
•When: August 6, 2026 at 8:00 A.M. Eastern Time (5:00 A.M. Pacific Time)
•Dial in: To access the call in the U.S., please register here. Callers are encouraged to dial into the call 10 to 15 minutes prior to the start to prevent any delay in joining.
•Webcast: https://investors.datadoghq.com (live and replay)
•Replay: A replay of the call will be archived on the investor relations website
Datadog is the leading observability and security platform for the AI era, providing businesses with unified visibility across the technology stack to manage complexity at scale. It brings applications, infrastructure, data, models, and security into one place, using AI to detect and resolve issues before they impact customers. Trusted globally by Fortune 500 companies and high-growth AI leaders, Datadog enables businesses to move faster with clarity and confidence.

Amphenol Rides on Communications Growth: Can AI Sustain Momentum?
Amphenol APH is benefiting from robust growth in its Communications Solutions segment, supported by accelerating demand for high-speed interconnect products used in AI infrastructure and contributions from its acquisition program. In the second quarter of 2026, Communications Solutions revenues surged 85% year over year to $5.38 billion and increased 42% organically. The segment accounted for roughly 62% of Amphenol's total revenues, making it the company's largest growth engine. The year-over-year growth was primarily driven by outsized IT datacom growth, particularly AI-related applications, alongside strength in industrial, mobile devices and automotive markets.
AI infrastructure remains the biggest growth engine and is helping the company fight off competition from the likes of TE Connectivity TEL and Bel Fuse BELFB. IT datacom represented 43% of Amphenol's second-quarter sales, with revenues rising 89% year over year and 63% organically. Sequentially, IT datacom revenues climbed 22%, with virtually all of the sequential growth stemming from AI-related products. APH expects another mid-teens sequential increase in the third quarter of 2026, supported by accelerating investments in AI data centers and stronger enterprise and cloud demand for traditional IT datacom equipment.
Amphenol's broad portfolio across high-speed copper, fiber-optic and power interconnects is strengthening its exposure to the AI buildout. The company noted that customers increasingly require all three technologies as computing architectures become denser and more power-intensive. The CommScope acquisition is further strengthening Communications Solutions, particularly in optical interconnects. CommScope generated slightly more than $1.2 billion in second-quarter sales, while its IT datacom business nearly doubled year over year. Amphenol now expects CommScope to generate $4.6 billion of sales in 2026, up from its earlier expectation of $4.1 billion.
Higher Communications Solutions revenues are also supporting profitability. Segment operating margin expanded to 33.6% in the second quarter of 2026 from 30.6% a year earlier, benefiting primarily from operating leverage on significantly higher organic volumes. This combination of accelerating AI connectivity demand, rising optical exposure through CommScope and strength across several other end markets should continue to support Communications Solutions as an important growth driver for Amphenol.
For the third quarter of 2026, APH expects sales of $9.3-$9.4 billion. The range implies year-over-year growth of 50-52%, assuming current market conditions and constant exchange rates. Adjusted earnings are projected between $1.40 and $1.42 per share, indicating growth of 51-53% from the prior-year quarter.
TE Connectivity is challenging Amphenol across high-speed data and power connectivity by expanding its exposure to AI infrastructure. TEL's Digital Data Networks (DDN) business is benefiting from hyperscaler investments in GPU clusters, with year-to-date DDN orders up more than 70%. In the third quarter of fiscal 2026, DDN sales increased 34% year over year, supported by demand for high-speed copper connectivity, while higher-voltage architectures are expanding opportunities in power connectivity. TE Connectivity estimates that power already represents roughly one-third of its DDN business, giving it exposure to both data transmission and rising power requirements inside AI racks.
Bel Fuse is a smaller but growing challenger. The company's Industrial Technology & Data Solutions (ITDS) segment includes power supplies, fuses, integrated connector modules and transformers used in networking, data centers and AI applications. In the second quarter of 2026, ITDS revenues jumped 31.1% year over year to $100.2 million, while Data Solutions revenues surged 55%, aided by the beginning of a ramp tied to high-performance computing project wins. The dataMate acquisition also expanded Bel Fuse's Data Solutions portfolio.
APH's Share Price Performance, Valuation & Estimates
Amphenol's shares have surged 24.8% year to date, outperforming the broader Zacks Computer & Technology sector's return of 21.8%.
Amphenol shares are trading at a premium, as suggested by a Value Score of D. In terms of the forward 12-month price-to-earnings (P/E), APH is trading at 27.47X, higher than the broader sector's 19.95X.
The Zacks Consensus Estimate for Amphenol's 2026 earnings is pegged at $2.66 per share, up three cents over the past 30 days. The figure indicates a 59.3% jump year over year.

Amphenol Aerospace’s AP-93-plated MIL-DTL-38999 Series III connectors are now available from FDH Electronics, providing a cadmium-free connector option for aerospace and defence systems. The AP-93 finish is the first RoHS-compliant D38999 connector finish approved by the US Defense Logistics Agency (DLA) for the Class AA designation.
For eeNews Europe readers designing high-reliability interconnect systems, the Class AA qualification provides a route away from cadmium finishes while retaining compatibility with existing MIL-DTL-38999 connectors.
Class AA is a service class within the MIL-DTL-38999 specification for Series III connector configurations. Amphenol Aerospace is currently the only manufacturer qualified to supply connectors under the new Qualified Products List (QPL) class, according to FDH Electronics.
The AP-93 finish uses a conductive tri-nickel alloy developed for aluminium connectors. Qualified MIL-DTL-38999 products carry the Class AA designation, while corresponding Amphenol commercial products use the DS service class.
AP-93 is both RoHS and REACH compliant and is intended for aerospace, defence and industrial applications where programs are seeking to reduce the use of restricted substances.
Salt spray resistance reaches 1,000 hours
The AP-93 connectors meet a 1,000-hour dynamic salt spray requirement, compared with the 500-hour performance specified by FDH for olive-drab cadmium Class W finishes. They are also rated for 500 mating cycles under MIL-DTL-38999 requirements and operating temperatures up to 200°C.
Shell-to-shell conductivity is specified at less than 2.5 mV, while the finish is non-magnetic. AP-93 is available for MIL-DTL-38999 Series III /20, /24 and /26 shell styles.
An important feature for existing systems is intermateability with cadmium-plated MIL-DTL-38999 connectors. This allows AP-93 components to be introduced into some legacy designs without replacing the corresponding mating interface.
Connectors address harsh-environment systems
The Class AA connectors are intended for systems exposed to salt, moisture, vibration and temperature extremes. Applications include military and commercial aircraft, naval platforms, ground vehicles, missile systems, satellites, unmanned platforms and high-reliability industrial equipment.

The unglamorous plumbing of the AI era rarely makes headlines, yet it is precisely where Amphenol has built its case. Connectors, sensors and high-speed cabling may lack the allure of chip design, but without them even the fastest processor sits idle. That physical reality is what keeps drawing investors back to the stock — and what pushed it to a fresh 52-week high of EUR 78.23 during Friday's session before it closed at EUR 77.28.
No single company announcement explained Friday's advance. Market watchers, as reported in the media, pointed instead to two structural forces: unrelenting demand tied to the global build-out of AI infrastructure, and the growing contribution of recently completed acquisitions. The shares have now climbed 32% since the start of the year, leaving them within striking distance of record territory.
Evidence that management is putting money behind that demand came from upstate New York. On September 23, the Delaware County Board of Supervisors passed a formal resolution backing Amphenol Aerospace, smoothing the company's path to the regulatory approvals it needs for a planned expansion of an electroplating facility in Sidney, New York.
The move reads like a local footnote but carries strategic weight. Active support from regional decision-makers reduces regulatory friction for an industrial project, and for the aerospace and defense division the site expansion locks in critical production steps needed to serve sustained demand.
Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying Amphenol?
Amphenol's growth story does not rest on classic IT alone. On September 22, Amphenol Ltd unveiled specialized interconnect solutions for electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft, or eVTOLs. The portfolio spans lightweight signal and power systems along with the high-voltage Raptor and Condor connectors. No major order accompanied the launch, but the push signals an intent to share in the electrification of aviation.
Days earlier, on September 15, Amphenol Ltd joined the British robotics initiative RAISE-SE as a consortium partner, an effort aimed at building expertise in automation technology. Taken together, the two moves show a company embedding itself early in industrial ecosystems where sophisticated sensing and rugged connectors will become indispensable.
The broader positioning has drawn a mixed reception on Wall Street. Bernstein initiated coverage on September 22 with an Outperform rating and a USD 99 price target. On Wednesday, Wolfe Research opened its own coverage at Outperform, setting a target of USD 105.00 — implying meaningful upside from current levels.
Not everyone is cheering. Zacks Research downgraded the stock from Strong Buy to Hold on Monday, according to media reports, a pause that surprises few after the run-up. Two other events had already stirred the pot: a 2-for-1 stock split implemented roughly a month ago, since which the shares have added 9.5%, and Citi's addition of the name to its watch list about three weeks back, a move accompanied by a 13.6% gain.
The split itself changed nothing about the company's value — it merely reset the share count, and the subsequent price moves should be read in that light rather than as evidence of any shift in sentiment. What matters more is the valuation math. After the recent highs, the market is pricing in a flawless continuation of growth, and the room for operational stumbles has narrowed.
For the current level to hold, the tailwinds from AI infrastructure and the newer industrial verticals must translate into hard earnings contributions in the coming reporting periods. The industrial groundwork — from Sidney's plating lines to eVTOL connectors and robotics consortia — appears to be in place. Whether the results arrive on schedule is now the question investors are paying up to answer.
